description:
Reading a file that the same command is writing: `grep`, `sed` and `head -c` must not read
forever, filling the disk and ignoring `timeout`/the call's time limit the way a real OS process
would respect SIGTERM.

`cat f >> f` is already refused this way (see streaming.rs); these are the same hazard in the
other commands whose own read loop can see the just-appended bytes before the call ends.

cases.name: growing file: grep -r refuses when a discovered target is the redirected output
cases.script: mkdir w; cd w; echo x > a; grep -r x . > out; echo status=$?

cases.name: growing file: grep refuses a named file that is the redirected output
cases.script: mkdir w; cd w; echo x > a; grep x a > a; echo status=$?

cases.name: growing file: sed honors timeout instead of reading its own output forever
cases.script: mkdir w; cd w; echo x > a; timeout 2 sed p a >> a; echo status=$?

expected.reason: fixture: GNU sed/head have no same-file check, so the oracle finishes almost instantly by accident of its own stdio buffering instead of looping; bash-tool's own loop now yields so `timeout` can end it instead, which is the fix (see README.md's Limits section)

cases.name: growing file: head -c honors timeout and never reaches its full count
cases.script: mkdir w; cd w; echo x > a; timeout 2 head -c 100000000 a >> a; echo status=$?

expected.reason: fixture: GNU sed/head have no same-file check, so the oracle finishes almost instantly by accident of its own stdio buffering instead of looping; bash-tool's own loop now yields so `timeout` can end it instead, which is the fix (see README.md's Limits section)
